Fire of the Spirit
FYR of the SPIR-it
n. phrase
From the cloven tongues "like as of fire" that sat upon the disciples at Pentecost (Acts 2:3); fire from Old English fýr, a common biblical emblem of God's purifying, illuminating, and consuming presence.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Fire of the Spirit is a scriptural figure for the Holy Ghost's purifying, illuminating, and zeal-kindling work, drawn chiefly from Pentecost, where there appeared unto the disciples "cloven tongues like as of fire," and it sat upon each of them (Acts 2:3). John the Baptist had foretold that the Messiah would baptize "with the Holy Ghost, and with fire" (Matt 3:11). The figure must be read by the analogy of faith, not by enthusiasm. Fire in Scripture signifies several settled realities of the Spirit's ministry. First, purification: as the refiner's fire purges dross from silver, so the Spirit sanctifies the saints, burning away corruption and conforming them to Christ. Second, illumination: fire gives light, and the Spirit enlightens the understanding to behold the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ as that glory shines forth from the written word. Third, zeal: the disciples were set ablaze for the proclamation of the gospel, their hearts burning within them. The apostolic charge therefore runs, "Quench not the Spirit" (1 Thess 5:19)—a man may, by sloth, neglect, or cherished sin, damp and stifle the Spirit's gracious operations as water quenches a flame. Yet this fire is not raw emotionalism, nor the manufactured frenzy of the revival-bench, nor a fresh revelation added to the closed canon. The Spirit's fire always burns along the channel of the word He Himself inspired; He kindles holy affections toward the truths of Scripture, never apart from them. To seek the "fire" as an experience detached from the word and the means of grace is to chase a strange fire the Lord hath not commanded. This dictionary confesses the Spirit's fire as the heart-warming, sin-purging, word-illuminating zeal of God in His people, ever subject to and proved by the sufficient and closed Scriptures.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 treats FIRE as the effect of combustion, giving heat and light, and figuratively as ardor of affection or zeal. The Fire of the Spirit is the Holy Ghost's purifying, illuminating, and zeal-kindling work, emblematized in the Pentecostal tongues of fire (Acts 2:3).

expand to see more

FIRE, n. — The effect of combustion. The combustion of inflammable substances, producing heat and light. Figuratively, ardor of affection; the heat or warmth of zeal or animation.

In the spiritual sense, the Fire of the Spirit is the Holy Ghost's sanctifying and illuminating presence, appearing at Pentecost as cloven tongues "like as of fire" resting upon the disciples (Acts 2:3).

"And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them" (Acts 2:3).

The figure requires the purging of dross, the giving of light to the understanding, and the kindling of holy zeal—and forbids the quenching of the Spirit by sloth or cherished sin (1 Thess 5:19).

It is no warrant for emotionalism or fresh revelation, but the heart-warming zeal of God exercised always along the channel of His written and sufficient word.

📖 Key Scripture

Acts 2:3 — "And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them."

Matthew 3:11 — "I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire."

1 Thessalonians 5:19 — "Quench not the Spirit."

Luke 24:32 — "And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Fire of the Spirit is corrupted when it is reduced to worked-up emotionalism or claimed as a fresh, canon-supplementing revelation, both of which detach the Spirit's work from the word He inspired.

expand to see more

The chief abuse of this figure is the substitution of emotional heat for the Spirit's genuine work. Whole movements have taught the saints to seek "the fire" as a felt experience—a quickened pulse, a flood of feeling, a frenzy at the altar—treating the intensity of the sensation as the measure of the Spirit's presence. But Scripture nowhere makes feeling the test of the Spirit; it makes the word the test of feeling. The Spirit's fire purifies from sin and conforms to Christ; where there is much heat and little holiness, the fire is strange and not from heaven. Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire which the Lord commanded not, and were consumed. The remedy is to seek the Spirit at the means He has appointed—the preached and read word, the sacraments, prayer—and to test every supposed kindling by the fruit of the Spirit and the doctrine of Scripture.

A second corruption claims the Spirit's fire as a fresh outpouring that adds new revelation to the church, as though the canon were still open and God were yet speaking words to be received with the authority of Scripture. This dictionary is cessationist: the Spirit no longer gives new inspired words, for the faith was once delivered unto the saints and the Scriptures are complete and sufficient. The fire that burns in true believers is the same Spirit applying the same finished word to the heart, making the saints' hearts burn within them as the Scriptures are opened (Luke 24:32). To recover the doctrine is to seek a holy, word-fed zeal—not visions, prophecies, or revelations, but a heart set aflame with love to the God who has already spoken fully in His Son and in the closed canon.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The figure rests on the Pentecostal tongues of fire (Acts 2:3) and the Old Testament emblem of fire as God's purifying and illuminating presence, behind the Greek pyr and the Hebrew esh.

expand to see more

Greek pyr (G4442) — fire; the element of the Pentecostal tongues and a frequent emblem of divine presence and judgment.

Hebrew 'esh (H784) — fire; the pillar of fire, the burning bush, the refiner's fire of God's purifying dealings.

Greek zēlos (G2205) — zeal, fervor; the holy ardor the Spirit kindles in the saints toward God and His truth.

Greek sbennymi (G4570) — to quench, extinguish; the verb of 1 Thess 5:19, warning against stifling the Spirit's operations.

The figure is always governed by the word: the Spirit's fire burns along the channel of the Scripture He inspired, never apart from it.

Usage

"The preacher prayed that the Fire of the Spirit would purge his own dross before he dared to handle the word in the pulpit."

"What passed for the Fire of the Spirit at the meeting was mere emotional heat, untested by Scripture and barren of holiness."

""Quench not the Spirit"—the saint is charged not to damp the Fire of the Spirit by sloth or cherished sin."
